questions.q: What are the two main structural parts of the chapter "The Interview" and what is the primary purpose of each part?
questions.a: The two parts are: Part I — an expository essay that surveys the history, definitions, and conflicting opinions about interviews; Part II — a verbatim interview with Umberto Eco that illustrates the genre in action. A wrong answer (e.g., "both parts are interviews" or "Part I is a story") reveals the student has not distinguished between the meta-discussion *about* interviews and the *instance* of an interview.

questions.q: In Part I, the author writes: "V. S. Naipaul 'feels that some people are wounded by interviews and lose a part of themselves,' Lewis Carroll... was said to have had 'a just horror of the interviewer'...". Explain how the repetition of celebrity names and the phrase "interviewer" functions as a linker in this paragraph.
questions.a: The repetition of "interviewer" and the listing of famous writers (Naipaul, Carroll, Kipling, Wells, Bellow) create a lexical chain that binds the examples together, showing they are all evidence for the same claim: celebrities often despise interviews. A wrong answer that only says "it gives examples" misses the cohesive function — the repeated vocabulary *is* the structural glue that makes the paragraph a unified argument rather than a random list.

questions.q:
Apply the concept of "signallers" to the following exchange from Part II and identify the signaller:  
Mukund: "Which brings me to my next question. The Name of the Rose is a very serious novel..."  
Eco: "No. Journalists are puzzled."  
What does the signaller "Which brings me to my next question" achieve in the interview's narrative flow?
questions.a: It explicitly marks a topic shift from Eco's writing habits to the reception of *The Name of the Rose*, preparing the listener/reader for a new line of inquiry and maintaining conversational coherence. A wrong answer like "it is just polite" fails to recognize the structural role: without such signallers, the interview would feel disjointed, jumping abruptly between unrelated subjects.

questions.q: Compare the narrative pacing of Part I (essay) and Part II (interview). How does the sentence structure in each part reflect its purpose?
questions.a: Part I uses longer, complex sentences with subordinate clauses (e.g., "Since its invention a little over 130 years ago, the interview has become a commonplace of journalism") to build a measured, authoritative argument. Part II uses shorter, elliptical utterances, direct questions, and frequent turn-taking ("Mukund: ... Eco: ...") to mimic real-time conversation. A wrong answer that says "both are similar" overlooks how syntax enacts genre: the essay *argues*; the interview *enacts*.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of placing the actual interview (Part II) after the essay (Part I) rather than before it. Support your judgment with two textual reasons.
questions.a: Placing Part II after Part I is effective because: (1) Part I equips the reader with the critical vocabulary (e.g., "interviewing ordeal," "thumbprints on his windpipe") to analyze Eco's responses meta-cognitively; (2) the essay's closing line — "the interviewer holds a position of unprecedented power and influence" — sets up an expectation that the interview then tests and complicates (Eco resists that power by claiming "I am a professor who writes novels on Sundays"). A wrong answer that prefers the reverse order ignores the pedagogical design: theory first, then illustration.

questions.q: Create a 4-question mini-interview with a classmate about their hobby, using at least two signallers (e.g., "Which brings me to...", "Let me ask you...") and two linkers (e.g., repeating a key word, using a reference pronoun like "that"). Write the dialogue in the same format as Part II.
questions.a: A strong response will show: (i) clear Q/A format with speaker labels, (ii) at least two explicit signallers marking topic shifts, (iii) at least two linkers creating cohesion across turns (e.g., "You mentioned painting. *That* takes patience. *Painting* also requires..."). A weak response that lacks signallers will read like a disconnected list of questions; one that lacks linkers will feel like separate monologues rather than a conversation.
